question: A 5-week-old male infant is brought to the Emergency Department with the complaint of vomiting. His parents state he has been unable to keep normal feedings down for the past week and now has projectile non-bilious vomiting after each meal. He was given a short course of oral erythromycin at 4 days of life for suspected bacterial conjunctivitis. Physical examination is significant for sunken fontanelles and dry mucous membranes. A palpable, ball shaped mass is noted just to the right of the epigastrum. Which of the following conditions is most likely in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Projectile non-bilious vomiting" -> "Palpable mass in epigastrum" -> "History of erythromycin use" -> "Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis" -> 95%
CHAIN: "Projectile non-bilious vomiting" -> "Sunken fontanelles" -> "Dehydration" -> "Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis" -> 90%
CHAIN: "Projectile non-bilious vomiting" -> "Palpable mass" -> "Infant age 5 weeks" -> "Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis" -> 92%
CHAIN: "Projectile non-bilious vomiting" -> "Non-bilious" -> "Obstruction before bile duct" -> "Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis" -> 88%
CHAIN: "Projectile non-bilious vomiting" -> "Palpable mass" -> "Right of epigastrum" -> "Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis" -> 93%
analysis: The infant presents with projectile non-bilious vomiting, dehydration signs (sunken fontanelles and dry mucous membranes), and a palpable mass in the epigastric region. These symptoms are classic for hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, a condition where the pylorus muscle thickens, obstructing gastric outflow. The history of erythromycin use is a known risk factor for developing this condition. Other options like gastroesophageal reflux, milk-protein allergy, midgut volvulus, and intussusception do not align as closely with the symptomatology and physical findings.
